texto.periodico: Journal of Collegiate Health and Learning (2026) 14, 211–236
texto.titulo: Evening screen use, sleep quality and academic performance in undergraduate students: a semester-long prospective study
texto.autores: L. Ferrandi-Okafor, J. Haldorsen-Teague and P. Ndlovu-Arriaga
texto.abstract: Insufficient and poor-quality sleep is widespread among university students, and evening use of screen-based devices is frequently blamed for it, yet the evidence linking the two to academic outcomes rests largely on cross-sectional surveys and self-reported grades. This study examined whether sleep duration, sleep quality and evening screen use predicted end-of-semester grade point average (GPA) among undergraduate students, and whether the association between screen use and grades was mediated by sleep. A total of 547 students at a public university completed a baseline questionnaire, a seven-day sleep and screen diary and a follow-up survey, and their GPAs were obtained from academic records; a subsample of 148 also wore wrist actigraphs. Sleep quality, but not sleep duration, predicted GPA once prior achievement and covariates were controlled for. Interactive evening screen use was indirectly associated with lower GPA through poorer sleep quality, whereas passive viewing was not, and the association was stronger among students with an evening chronotype. The findings suggest that interventions aimed at student sleep should target the quality of sleep and the kind of screen activity rather than total screen time alone.
texto.keywords: sleep quality, screen use, chronotype, academic performance, undergraduate students

blocos.p: Sleep problems are among the most commonly reported health complaints in university populations. Surveys conducted over the past two decades have repeatedly found that a substantial proportion of undergraduates sleep less than the seven to nine hours recommended for young adults, and that many of them describe their sleep as unrefreshing, fragmented or irregular (Halvorsen-Pike, 2013; Okereke-Lund, 2018). The transition to university is thought to be particularly disruptive, given that it typically coincides with a loss of parental supervision, irregular class schedules, part-time employment and a social life that is concentrated in the late evening. Since the early 2010s, moreover, smartphones, laptops and tablets have been steadily colonising the period between dinner and sleep, and they are now used for coursework, communication and entertainment alike. It is therefore unsurprising that evening screen use has come to be regarded, both in the popular press and in campus health campaigns, as one of the principal culprits behind students’ poor sleep and, by extension, behind disappointing academic results.

Two accounts of how screens might interfere with sleep can be distinguished in the literature. The first, which may be termed the displacement account, holds that time spent on devices simply replaces time that would otherwise have been spent asleep: students who stay online go to bed later but still have to rise for morning classes, and their sleep is shortened accordingly. The second, the arousal account, attributes the harm not to the amount of time consumed but to what happens during it, namely the cognitive and emotional stimulation produced by messaging, gaming and scrolling through social media, together with the alerting effect of the short-wavelength light emitted by screens. Whereas the former predicts that screen use should affect sleep duration above all, the latter predicts that it should affect sleep quality, that is, how long it takes to fall asleep, how often one wakes during the night and how rested one feels in the morning. These predictions have rarely been tested against each other, since most studies have measured screen use as a single global quantity.

The association between sleep and academic achievement has been examined in a considerable number of studies, albeit with inconsistent results. In one of the earliest large surveys of its kind, Marchetti-Oyelaran (2014) reported that students who habitually slept fewer than six hours on weeknights had a grade point average 0.34 points lower, on a four-point scale, than those who slept seven hours or more, and concluded that sleep duration was the critical variable. Lindgaard and Soto-Brannagh (2017), by contrast, found that once sleep quality had been entered into their models, duration no longer made a significant contribution to grades; in their view, it is not how long students sleep but how well they sleep that matters for learning, given that memory consolidation depends on uninterrupted deep sleep rather than on time spent in bed. A third position was advanced by Achterhof-Bianchi (2019), who argued that the irregularity of sleep schedules, rather than either duration or quality, is what most consistently distinguishes low-achieving students, and that the global measures used in most surveys tend to conceal it.

Research on screens has followed a similar trajectory. Vasquez-Holm et al. (2019), in a sample of 1,036 students, observed that each additional hour of screen use in the two hours preceding bedtime was associated with a 21-minute delay in sleep onset, an effect they attributed primarily to light exposure. Their interpretation was challenged by Ebrahimi-Castro (2020), who, in a laboratory study involving 64 students, found that participants who read e-books on backlit tablets fell asleep almost as quickly as those who read printed books, whereas the ones who exchanged messages before bed took considerably longer; he concluded that the content of screen activity, rather than the light emitted, accounts for most of the effect. Thornbury-Achebe (2016) had earlier cautioned that nearly all of this evidence is cross-sectional and that the direction of causality cannot be taken for granted: students who sleep badly may turn to their phones because they cannot sleep, rather than sleeping badly because they use their phones.

Three limitations of the existing literature motivated the present study. First, academic performance has usually been measured by students’ own reports of their grades, which are known to be inflated, particularly among low achievers (Delacroix-Nwosu, 2018). Second, sleep and screen use have mostly been assessed with single retrospective questions, which are vulnerable to recall bias and cannot separate the different kinds of activity that take place on a screen. Third, few studies have followed the same students over time, so that the temporal ordering of screen use, sleep and achievement has seldom been established. The present study addressed these limitations by combining a seven-day diary with wrist actigraphy in a subsample, by obtaining grades directly from academic records and by following a cohort of undergraduates across a full semester.

The study was guided by four research questions: (1) To what extent do sleep duration and sleep quality, measured early in the semester, predict end-of-semester GPA once prior achievement is controlled for? (2) Is evening screen use associated with sleep duration, sleep quality, or both, and does the association differ between interactive and passive screen activities? (3) Is the association between evening screen use and GPA mediated by sleep? (4) Are these associations moderated by chronotype, that is, by students’ preference for morning or evening activity?

Participants were recruited from a public university of approximately 22,000 students located in a mid-sized city. All 1,284 first- and second-year undergraduates enrolled in four faculties (health sciences, engineering, humanities and business) during the first semester of 2024 were invited by e-mail to take part, and 612 completed the baseline questionnaire. Of these, 547 (89.4%) also completed the diary and the follow-up survey and consented to the release of their grades, and they constitute the analytic sample. Their mean age was 20.3 years (SD = 2.1); 336 (61.4%) were women, and 41.7% were in their first year. Just over a third (35.1%) reported paid work of at least ten hours per week, most of them employed off-campus. Students who had been diagnosed with a sleep disorder or who worked night shifts were excluded at baseline, and those who completed only the baseline questionnaire did not differ significantly from the analytic sample in age, gender or prior GPA.

Sleep quality was assessed with the Campus Sleep Quality Scale (CSQS), a 12-item instrument developed by Okereke-Lund (2018) for student populations, which covers sleep latency, night-time awakenings, perceived depth of sleep and daytime tiredness. Items are rated on a four-point scale, yielding a total score from 0 to 36, with higher scores indicating better sleep; internal consistency in the present sample was good (Cronbach’s α = .84). Chronotype was measured with the six-item Morning–Evening Preference Index, on the basis of which students were classified as morning, intermediate or evening types. Sleep duration and evening screen use were recorded in a structured online diary which was completed each morning, just as students got up, for seven consecutive days. For each evening, students reported the time at which they turned off the lights, their estimated time of falling asleep and their time of waking, as well as the minutes spent on screens in the two hours before lights-out, which were divided into interactive activities (messaging, social media and gaming) and passive activities (watching videos or films and reading).

To check the accuracy of self-reported sleep duration, a randomly selected subsample of 160 participants was invited to wear a wrist actigraph throughout the diary week; 148 provided usable data, the remainder having removed the device for more than one night. Academic performance was operationalised as the GPA for the semester, on a scale from 0 to 10, which was obtained directly from the university registry with the written consent of each student. Prior achievement was indexed by the GPA of the preceding semester or, for first-year students, by the standardised score in the university entrance examination. Weekly hours of paid work, daily caffeine intake and gender were recorded as covariates.

Data were collected in three waves. The baseline questionnaire, which included the CSQS, the chronotype index and the demographic items, was administered online in the third week of the semester. The diary week was scheduled for the fifth week, a period that had been chosen because it contained no examinations or public holidays and could therefore be regarded as typical of the teaching weeks. The follow-up survey was completed in the final week of classes, and grades were retrieved from the registry six weeks later, once all marks had been confirmed. Questionnaires were linked by a code generated by each participant, so that no names were stored with the data, and the registry released grades only against these codes. Students received a voucher worth the equivalent of a meal on completing each wave. The protocol had been approved by the institutional ethics committee before recruitment began.

Hierarchical linear regression was used to address the first question, with prior achievement, gender, paid work and caffeine intake entered in the first step and the sleep variables in the second. For the second question, sleep duration and CSQS scores were regressed on interactive and passive screen time separately. Mediation was tested with a bootstrap procedure using 5,000 resamples, and indirect effects were considered significant provided that the 95% confidence interval did not include zero. Moderation by chronotype was examined by adding interaction terms to the mediation models. As diary data were missing for some evenings, weekly means were computed only for participants who had completed at least five of the seven entries; this criterion was met by 531 of the 547 students.

On weeknights, participants reported sleeping a mean of 6 h 41 min (SD = 58 min), and 43.2% slept less than seven hours on average; on weekend nights, mean duration rose to 8 h 05 min. The midpoint of sleep was, on average, 84 minutes later at weekends than on weekdays. In the actigraphy subsample, self-reported duration exceeded the actigraphic estimate by a mean of 23 minutes, although the two measures were strongly correlated (r = .78); students must have overestimated how long they slept, yet they ranked themselves accurately relative to one another. The mean CSQS score was 21.6 (SD = 5.9), and a substantial minority of students (28.9%) scored below 18, a threshold that has been associated with clinically relevant sleep complaints in earlier validation work (Okereke-Lund, 2018). Evening chronotypes accounted for 39.5% of the sample, morning types for 14.8% and intermediate types for the remainder.

Screen use in the two hours preceding lights-out averaged 78 minutes per evening (SD = 27), of which 49 minutes were spent on interactive and 29 minutes on passive activities. Almost all participants (96.2%) used a screen nightly throughout the diary week, and 71.8% reported using their phone in bed after the lights had been turned off on at least four of the seven nights. Interactive use was concentrated among younger students and evening types, whereas passive use varied comparatively little across groups. Messaging and social media were the interactive activities most frequently reported by evening-type students; gaming, by contrast, was concentrated in a small group of heavy users. Notably, the diary revealed a highly irregular nightly pattern of interactive screen use, with peaks on Sunday and Thursday evenings, which roughly corresponded to the eves of the days on which most assignments were due.

Table 1 summarises the hierarchical regression predicting semester GPA. Prior achievement, gender, paid work and caffeine intake together accounted for 31.4% of the variance in the first step, prior achievement being by far the strongest predictor (β = .52, p < .001). Adding the sleep variables in the second step increased the explained variance to 36.0% (ΔR² = .046, p < .001). In this step, CSQS score was a significant predictor (β = .19, p < .001), whereas weeknight sleep duration was not (β = .06, p = .17), and the weekday–weekend difference in sleep midpoint made a small negative contribution (β = −.09, p = .02). Put in practical terms, a student scoring one standard deviation above the mean on the CSQS could be expected to obtain a GPA approximately 0.31 points higher, on the ten-point scale, than an otherwise comparable student scoring at the mean. When the actigraphic estimate was substituted for self-reported duration in the subsample, duration again failed to reach significance, which suggests that the null result for duration is not simply an artefact of self-report.

With regard to the second research question, interactive screen time was negatively associated with CSQS scores (β = −.28, p < .001) and, more weakly, with weeknight sleep duration (β = −.12, p = .006), whereas passive screen time was associated with neither (β = −.04 and β = −.03, respectively). In the mediation models, the indirect effect of interactive screen use on GPA through sleep quality was significant (ab = −.053, 95% CI [−.081, −.029]), while the indirect path through sleep duration was not, its confidence interval including zero. The direct effect of interactive screen use on GPA, which was subsequently estimated with sleep quality held constant, was small and non-significant, suggesting that most of the association between interactive use and grades was carried by poorer sleep quality. No indirect effect was found for passive use.

Chronotype moderated the first link in this chain. Among evening types, each additional 30 minutes of interactive screen use was associated with a 1.4-point reduction in CSQS score, compared with 0.6 points among intermediate types; among morning types, the association did not reach significance, a result which should be read with caution given that this group comprised only 81 students. Consequently, the indirect effect on GPA was approximately twice as large for evening types as for the sample as a whole. Gender did not moderate any of the associations, and the pattern of results was unchanged when students in paid employment were analysed separately.

The most robust finding of this study is that the quality of students’ sleep, rather than its duration, predicted their grades at the end of the semester. This pattern is consistent with that reported by Lindgaard and Soto-Brannagh (2017) and at odds with the conclusion drawn by Marchetti-Oyelaran (2014), although the discrepancy may be smaller than it appears. It is often argued that short sleep and poor sleep are simply two faces of the same problem; in the present sample, however, the two were only moderately correlated (r = .29), and a sizeable group of students slept fewer than seven hours while nonetheless reporting good sleep quality. Had Marchetti-Oyelaran’s survey included a measure of quality, part of the effect attributed to duration might well have been absorbed by it. It must also be borne in mind that the range of durations observed here was relatively narrow, so that the effects of severe sleep restriction, which is less common among students than is frequently assumed, could not have been detected.

With regard to evening screen use, the results lend more support to the arousal account than to the displacement account. Interactive use was associated mainly with poorer sleep quality and only weakly with shorter sleep, and passive use, which presumably involves the same exposure to screen light as interactive use, was associated with neither. Since the harmful association was confined to interactive activities, it seems unlikely that light exposure alone can explain it; this interpretation is in line with Ebrahimi-Castro (2020), who had reached a similar conclusion in a laboratory setting, albeit with a much smaller sample. Messaging and social media, unlike a film, do not come to a natural end, and their content is often emotionally charged; they may thus keep students cognitively engaged well beyond the moment at which they intend to sleep. Notwithstanding these considerations, the possibility of reverse causality raised by Thornbury-Achebe (2016) cannot be ruled out: students who were already sleeping poorly may have reached for their phones because they were unable to fall asleep.

The moderating role of chronotype deserves particular attention. Evening types, who made up nearly two-fifths of the sample, were both the heaviest users of interactive media and the students whose sleep quality was most sensitive to it. One plausible explanation is that, for students whose biological clock already inclines them to fall asleep late, an additional source of arousal pushes sleep onset into the small hours, whereas morning types tend to become drowsy regardless of what they are doing on their phones. Given that early morning classes are common in the first years of most degree programmes, evening types are also those whose sleep is most likely to be curtailed by the timetable, and the combination of late onset and early rising may compound the effect of poorer sleep quality.

These findings have implications for the design of interventions. Campus campaigns have typically urged students to reduce their total screen time or to use night-mode filters that lower the emission of blue light. The present results suggest that such advice is unlikely to be effective unless it is directed at the kind of activity in which students engage: a student who watches a film in the hour before bed may be at no greater risk than one who merely reads a printed book, whereas one who spends the same hour messaging may be at considerably greater risk. Brief interventions encouraging students to stop interactive use thirty minutes before lights-out, or to leave their phones outside the bedroom, could produce meaningful improvements in sleep quality, provided that they are targeted at evening types and are timed to precede the periods of heaviest academic workload. Whether such improvements would in turn translate into better grades remains, however, to be demonstrated.

Several limitations should be acknowledged. First, although the prospective design ensured that sleep quality was measured before grades were awarded, the study remains observational, and unmeasured variables such as conscientiousness or depressive symptoms could have influenced both sleep and achievement. Second, screen use was self-reported, and the time students spent on their phones may have been underestimated, as has been found when diary reports were compared with device logs (Pemberton-Ilori, 2021). Third, the diary covered a single week which, although it had been selected to be typical, may not have captured the variation that occurs around examination periods. Fourth, the sample was drawn from a single university, and the response rate at baseline was below 50%; students who chose to participate may have been more interested in sleep, or more conscientious, than those who did not. Finally, actigraphy was available for only about a quarter of the sample, so the conclusion that duration does not predict grades rests largely on self-reported data.

Future research could address these limitations in several ways. Experimental studies in which students are randomly assigned to restrict interactive use in the evening would allow causal conclusions to be drawn, and would show whether improvements in sleep quality translate into gains in achievement. Objective logging of device activity, which has become technically feasible with the consent of participants, would remove the reliance on self-report and allow the timing of use to be related precisely to sleep onset. Longitudinal designs covering several semesters, including examination periods, are also needed to establish whether the associations observed here are stable or vary with academic workload. Finally, replication in other countries and types of institution, particularly those in which students commute long distances or live with their parents, would clarify how far the present results can be generalised.

This study set out to clarify how evening screen use, sleep and academic performance are related in undergraduate students. Its central conclusion is that the quality of sleep, rather than the number of hours slept, is what predicts end-of-semester grades, and that evening screen use matters chiefly through its effect on sleep quality and only when it takes an interactive form. Passive viewing, which accounts for a large share of students’ evening screen time, showed no association with either sleep or grades. Campaigns that address screen time as a single undifferentiated quantity will therefore miss the distinction on which the present findings turn.

For universities, the practical lesson is that efforts to improve student sleep are likely to be more productive if they focus on what students do on their screens, and when, than on how long they use them. Such efforts should give priority to students with an evening chronotype, who appear to be the most vulnerable, and should be accompanied by a reconsideration of early morning timetabling in the first years of study. Since the associations reported here were modest in size and cannot be interpreted causally, sleep should be regarded as one contributor to academic success among many, not as a remedy for poor performance in itself.

questoes.explicacao:
O resumo diz: This study examined whether sleep duration, sleep quality and evening screen use predicted end-of-semester grade point average (GPA) among undergraduate students, and whether the association between screen use and grades was mediated by sleep. A alternativa (d) reproduz as variáveis, o público e a direção da mediação (o sono fica entre telas e notas).

Cada distrator muda um único elemento. (a) inverte a mediação: as notas seriam o elo entre telas e sono. (b) troca evening (“à noite”) por “ao longo do dia”. (c) troca o mediador: o cronotipo aparece no resumo, mas como moderador (the association was stronger among students with an evening chronotype), não como mediador. (e) acrescenta “autorrelatada”, quando o resumo diz que as notas foram obtidas from academic records e critica justamente os estudos com self-reported grades.
questoes.dica: Dica: quando as alternativas são quase idênticas, compare-as palavra por palavra com a frase do resumo que diz o que foi examinado. Confira o período (à noite × durante o dia), a fonte dos dados (registros × autorrelato) e o papel de cada variável: mediador (fica no meio do caminho entre X e Y) não é o mesmo que moderador (muda a força da relação).

questoes.enunciado: Os segmentos destacados em “Their interpretation was challenged by Ebrahimi-Castro (2020), who, in a laboratory study involving 64 students, found that participants who read e-books on backlit tablets fell asleep almost as quickly as those who read printed books, whereas the ones who exchanged messages before bed took considerably longer” (§4) referem-se, respectivamente, a
alternativas: 1,036 students – participants – participants
Vasquez-Holm et al. – participants – participants
Vasquez-Holm et al. – backlit tablets – participants
Vasquez-Holm et al. – participants – printed books
1,036 students – e-books – printed books
questoes.explicacao:
Their: a interpretação contestada é a de quem atribuiu o atraso no sono à luz, isto é, Vasquez-Holm et al. (2019), sujeito da frase anterior (an effect they attributed primarily to light exposure). 1,036 students (a, e) é o plural mais próximo, mas a amostra não tem “interpretação”.

those: a comparação é entre pessoas: participantes que leram em tablets adormeceram quase tão rápido quanto os participantes que leram livros impressos. Backlit tablets (c) e e-books (e) não “leem livros”.

the ones: ones substitui um substantivo contável já citado; quem trocou mensagens e demorou a dormir foram, de novo, os participantes. Printed books (d) é o plural imediatamente anterior, a armadilha da leitura apressada.
questoes.dica: Método: (1) para their no início de frase, procure o sujeito plural da frase anterior que possa “possuir” o substantivo (uma interpretação é de autores, não de amostras); (2) those who / the ones who retomam pessoas ou coisas da mesma categoria do termo comparado; (3) teste o verbo: quem “lê livros” ou “troca mensagens”? Desconfie do substantivo mais próximo.

questoes.enunciado:
Nos parágrafos 3 e 4, os autores apresentam achados e argumentos de estudos anteriores. Associe as colunas, relacionando cada afirmação a seu(s) respectivo(s) autor(es). Um dos autores não será utilizado.

  1. Marchetti-Oyelaran (2014)
  2. Lindgaard and Soto-Brannagh (2017)
  3. Achterhof-Bianchi (2019)
  4. Vasquez-Holm et al. (2019)
  5. Thornbury-Achebe (2016)
  • (  )Para aprender, importa mais dormir bem do que dormir muito, já que a consolidação da memória depende de sono profundo sem interrupções.
  • (  )As medidas globais de sono usadas na maioria dos levantamentos tendem a esconder o fator que mais diferencia os alunos de baixo desempenho.
  • (  )Mais tempo de tela nas horas anteriores ao deitar associou-se a demora para adormecer, efeito explicado sobretudo pela luz.
  • (  )Não se pode dar como certo que o celular piore o sono: quem dorme mal pode recorrer ao aparelho justamente por não conseguir dormir.

Assinale a sequência correta.
questoes.explicacao:
2: Lindgaard and Soto-Brannagh: it is not how long students sleep but how well they sleep that matters for learning, given that memory consolidation depends on uninterrupted deep sleep rather than on time spent in bed (§3).

3: Achterhof-Bianchi: the global measures used in most surveys tend to conceal it, sendo it a irregularidade dos horários, what most consistently distinguishes low-achieving students (§3). Quem lê às pressas associa “medidas globais” à dupla que defende a qualidade (a), mas são posições distintas.

4: Vasquez-Holm et al.: each additional hour of screen use in the two hours preceding bedtime was associated with a 21-minute delay in sleep onset, an effect they attributed primarily to light exposure (§4).

5: Thornbury-Achebe: the direction of causality cannot be taken for granted: students who sleep badly may turn to their phones because they cannot sleep (§4).

Sobra Marchetti-Oyelaran (1), que defendeu a duração como variável crítica; (b), (c) e (d) o encaixam no lugar de outro autor. (a) troca os dois autores do §3 que discordam de Marchetti-Oyelaran.
questoes.dica: Dica: as afirmações vêm parafraseadas; procure a ideia, não as palavras. Leia a frase inteira de cada autor, inclusive o que vem depois de who, in their view ou de dois-pontos. Quando um autor sobra, ele costuma ser o mais “óbvio” do parágrafo: confirme que nenhuma afirmação é dele antes de descartá-lo.

questoes.enunciado: Assinale a alternativa que NÃO corresponde a nenhuma das perguntas de pesquisa do estudo (§6).
alternativas: Controlado o desempenho anterior, em que grau a duração e a qualidade do sono, aferidas no começo do semestre, permitem prever a média final?
A relação entre o uso noturno de telas e o sono varia conforme a atividade na tela seja interativa ou passiva?
O gênero dos estudantes modera as associações entre o uso noturno de telas, o sono e a média de notas?
O sono funciona como elo intermediário entre o uso de telas à noite e a média do semestre?
A inclinação dos estudantes para a atividade matinal ou noturna altera a força dessas associações?
questoes.explicacao:
As alternativas parafraseiam as quatro perguntas do §6: (a) = (1) To what extent do sleep duration and sleep quality, measured early in the semester, predict end-of-semester GPA once prior achievement is controlled for?; (b) = parte de (2) does the association differ between interactive and passive screen activities?; (d) = (3) Is the association between evening screen use and GPA mediated by sleep?; (e) = (4) Are these associations moderated by chronotype, that is, by students’ preference for morning or evening activity?

(c) é o intruso, e é parecido com (e): a moderação perguntada é por cronotipo, não por gênero. O gênero aparece no estudo, mas como covariável (§9) e num resultado secundário (Gender did not moderate any of the associations, §16), não como pergunta de pesquisa.
questoes.dica: Dica: em “NÃO corresponde”, ache a lista numerada e marque cada alternativa com o número da pergunta, mesmo que esteja parafraseada (“elo intermediário” = mediação; “inclinação para a atividade matinal ou noturna” = cronotipo). O intruso costuma ser algo que o estudo de fato analisou, mas em outro papel (covariável, resultado secundário).

Sobre o método do estudo, indique se os segmentos a seguir estão em acordo (A) ou desacordo (D) com o que apresentam os parágrafos 7 a 10.

  • (  )Menos da metade dos estudantes da amostra analítica cursava o primeiro ano.
  • (  )A quinta semana foi reservada ao diário por não ter provas nem feriados, o que a tornava representativa das semanas de aula.
  • (  )Dos 160 estudantes sorteados para usar o actígrafo, 12 foram descartados por terem retirado o aparelho durante uma noite.
  • (  )Para os calouros, o desempenho prévio foi estimado pela média do semestre anterior.

Assinale a sequência correta.
alternativas: A – A – D – D
A – D – D – D
A – A – A – D
D – A – D – D
A – A – D – A
questoes.explicacao:
1 (A): 41.7% were in their first year (§7), ou seja, menos da metade. Não confunda com os 61,4% (mulheres) nem com os 35,1% (trabalho remunerado).

2 (A): The diary week was scheduled for the fifth week, a period that had been chosen because it contained no examinations or public holidays and could therefore be regarded as typical of the teaching weeks (§10).

3 (D): o número bate (160 − 148 = 12), mas o motivo não: the remainder having removed the device for more than one night (§9). Uma única noite não levava ao descarte.

4 (D): a média do semestre anterior valia para os demais; para calouros, usou-se a nota do vestibular: or, for first-year students, by the standardised score in the university entrance examination (§9).

Cada alternativa errada difere da certa em um só item, por isso é preciso conferir os quatro.
questoes.dica: Dica: nos itens sobre método, faça a conta quando o item converte números (41,7% → “menos da metade”; 160 − 148 = 12) e leia até o fim da frase: o detalhe que torna o item falso costuma estar no final (more than one night, for first-year students). Um item com número certo pode estar errado no motivo.

questoes.enunciado:
Considere os segmentos a seguir.

I - “Just over a third (35.1%) reported paid work of at least ten hours per week, most of them employed off-campus” (§7) II - “Almost all participants (96.2%) used a screen nightly throughout the diary week” (§13) III - “a student who watches a film in the hour before bed may be at no greater risk than one who merely reads a printed book” (§20)

Os segmentos sublinhados apresentam, respectivamente, ideia de
alternativas: lugar – tempo – restrição.
modo – frequência – restrição.
lugar – frequência – restrição.
lugar – frequência – modo.
lugar – tempo – modo.
questoes.explicacao:
I off-campus = “fora do campus”: diz onde os estudantes trabalhavam, ideia de lugar. Não é modo (b): não diz como trabalhavam.

II nightly = “todas as noites”, “a cada noite”: diz com que frequência usavam a tela, não em que momento. Por isso é frequência, e não tempo (a, e), embora a palavra contenha night. Compare com daily, weekly.

III merely = “apenas”, “simplesmente”: restringe a ação a ler um livro impresso, sem nada além disso. É restrição, não modo (d, e), apesar do -ly.
questoes.dica: Dica: classifique o advérbio pela pergunta que ele responde: onde? (lugar), quando? (tempo), com que frequência? (nightly, daily, seldom), como? (modo), quanto? (intensidade), “só isso”? (restrição: merely, only, solely). O sufixo -ly não garante modo, e uma palavra ligada a tempo (night) pode indicar frequência.

questoes.enunciado: O segmento destacado em “Messaging and social media were the interactive activities most frequently reported by evening-type students” (§13) pode ser traduzido, no contexto em que é empregado, por
alternativas: as atividades mais interativas relatadas com frequência pelos estudantes de cronotipo vespertino.
os estudantes de cronotipo vespertino que relataram com mais frequência atividades interativas.
as atividades interativas relatadas com frequência pelos estudantes de cronotipo mais vespertino.
as atividades interativas relatadas com mais frequência aos estudantes de cronotipo vespertino.
as atividades interativas relatadas com mais frequência pelos estudantes de cronotipo vespertino.
questoes.explicacao:
O núcleo é activities, modificado à esquerda por interactive (“atividades interativas”) e à direita por um particípio: reported (“relatadas”), que traz seu próprio advérbio, most frequently (“com mais frequência”), e o agente, by evening-type students (“pelos estudantes de cronotipo vespertino”). Resultado: (e).

(a) desloca most para interactive (“mais interativas”), mas most modifica frequently. (b) faz de students o núcleo e de reported um verbo ativo; o sujeito de were são as mídias, logo o núcleo tem de ser “atividades”. (c) pendura most em “vespertino”. (d) troca o agente (by = “por”) por um destinatário (“aos estudantes”).
questoes.dica: Dica: com particípio depois do núcleo (the X reported by Y, the data collected in Z), traduza como oração reduzida: “os X relatados por Y”. O advérbio que vem colado ao particípio (most frequently reported) modifica o particípio, não o adjetivo do núcleo. By depois de particípio introduz o agente (“por”).

questoes.enunciado:
Associe os dados numéricos apresentados nos Resultados (§12–§13) aos seus respectivos referentes. Um dos números não será utilizado.

  1. 23 minutos
  2. 29 minutos
  3. 84 minutos
  4. 28,9%
  5. 43,2%
  • (  )Tempo médio, por noite, dedicado a assistir a vídeos ou ler na tela antes de apagar as luzes.
  • (  )Quanto o sono declarado pelos estudantes superou, em média, o registrado pelo aparelho de pulso.
  • (  )Parcela de estudantes com pontuação de qualidade do sono abaixo de um limiar associado a queixas clinicamente relevantes.
  • (  )Defasagem média do ponto médio do sono entre fins de semana e dias úteis.

Assinale a sequência correta.
questoes.explicacao:
2: o uso passivo (passive activities (watching videos or films and reading), §8) somou 29 minutes por noite: of which 49 minutes were spent on interactive and 29 minutes on passive activities (§13).

1: self-reported duration exceeded the actigraphic estimate by a mean of 23 minutes (§12).

4: a substantial minority of students (28.9%) scored below 18, a threshold that has been associated with clinically relevant sleep complaints (§12).

3: The midpoint of sleep was, on average, 84 minutes later at weekends than on weekdays (§12).

Sobra o 5 (43,2%): é a proporção que dormia menos de sete horas nas noites de semana, um dado de duração, não de qualidade. (b) e (e) caem nessa troca; (a) e (e) invertem os dois valores próximos em minutos (23 e 29); (d) troca 23 por 84.
questoes.dica: Dica: os referentes vêm parafraseados (“aparelho de pulso” = actigraph; “assistir a vídeos ou ler” = passive activities). Ache primeiro o termo técnico correspondente e depois o número da mesma frase. Números próximos e da mesma unidade (23 × 29 minutos; 28,9% × 43,2%) são os que se trocam.

questoes.enunciado: A função do segmento destacado em “Notably, the diary revealed a highly irregular nightly pattern of interactive screen use, with peaks on Sunday and Thursday evenings” (§13) é
alternativas: retomar um resultado já apresentado anteriormente no mesmo parágrafo.
chamar a atenção para um dado que os autores julgam digno de destaque.
introduzir uma ressalva que limita o alcance do que foi dito antes.
apresentar uma conclusão que decorre dos dados descritos antes.
indicar que o resultado observado contraria o que se esperava.
questoes.explicacao:
Notably (“cabe notar”, “de modo digno de nota”) é um marcador de ênfase: destaca o dado seguinte, o padrão irregular com picos às vésperas dos prazos, como especialmente relevante. É (b).

(a) é a leitura apressada: o uso interativo já foi citado no parágrafo, mas o padrão por dia da semana é informação nova; retomar seria as noted above ou as mentioned. (c) Ressalva seria however, admittedly. (d) Conclusão seria thus, therefore. (e) Notably não significa “surpreendentemente” (surprisingly, unexpectedly): destaca, sem dizer que contraria uma expectativa.
questoes.dica: Dica: separe os marcadores pela função. Ênfase: notably, indeed, in particular, above all. Retomada: as noted above, as mentioned earlier. Ressalva/concessão: admittedly, however. Conclusão: thus, therefore. Surpresa: surprisingly. Teste a tradução no contexto; “notavelmente” engana, porque sugere surpresa.

questoes.enunciado:
Considere os segmentos a seguir.

I - “When the actigraphic estimate was substituted for self-reported duration in the subsample, duration again failed to reach significance, which suggests that the null result for duration is not simply an artefact of self-report” (§14) II - “passive screen time was associated with neither (β = −.04 and β = −.03, respectively)” (§15) III - “while the indirect path through sleep duration was not, its confidence interval including zero” (§15)

Os segmentos sublinhados referem-se, respectivamente, a
alternativas: o fato de a duração, mesmo medida por actigrafia, não ter sido significativa – CSQS scores e weeknight sleep duration – the indirect path through sleep duration
a estimativa actigráfica usada na subamostra – CSQS scores e weeknight sleep duration – the indirect path through sleep duration
o fato de a duração, mesmo medida por actigrafia, não ter sido significativa – weeknight sleep duration e CSQS scores – the indirect path through sleep duration
o fato de a duração, mesmo medida por actigrafia, não ter sido significativa – CSQS scores e weeknight sleep duration – sleep duration
a estimativa actigráfica usada na subamostra – interactive e passive screen time – the indirect path through sleep duration
questoes.explicacao:
I which, depois de vírgula, retoma aqui a oração inteira: o fato de a duração ter novamente falhado em atingir significância com a medida actigráfica é o que “sugere que o resultado nulo não é mero artefato do autorrelato”. A estimativa actigráfica (b, e) não “sugere” nada sozinha; é o resultado obtido com ela que sugere.

II respectively segue a ordem da frase anterior: interactive screen time was negatively associated with CSQS scores […] and, more weakly, with weeknight sleep duration; o uso passivo não se associou a nenhum dos dois, na mesma ordem (CSQS → −.04; duração → −.03). (c) inverte a ordem; (e) aponta os dois tipos de uso de tela, mas os betas são do uso passivo com cada desfecho.

III its retoma the indirect path through sleep duration: o intervalo de confiança é do efeito indireto (compare com ab = −.053, 95% CI […]). Sleep duration (d) é o substantivo mais próximo, mas é a variável, não o efeito estimado.
questoes.dica: Método: (1) which logo após vírgula e seguido de verbo como suggests, means, indicates costuma retomar toda a oração anterior (“o que sugere…”); (2) respectively exige localizar a lista original e manter a ordem; (3) para its, pergunte de quem é o atributo (intervalo de confiança é de uma estimativa, não de uma variável).

questoes.enunciado:
Considere os segmentos a seguir.

I - “a structured online diary which was completed each morning, just as students got up, for seven consecutive days” (§8) II - “As diary data were missing for some evenings, weekly means were computed only for participants who had completed at least five of the seven entries” (§11) III - “passive use, which presumably involves the same exposure to screen light as interactive use, was associated with neither” (§18)

Em I, II e III, o conector as estabelece, respectivamente, relação de
alternativas: causa – tempo – comparação.
tempo – causa – causa.
comparação – causa – comparação.
tempo – causa – comparação.
tempo – tempo – comparação.
questoes.explicacao:
I (tempo): just as students got up = “bem na hora em que os estudantes se levantavam”: marca o momento do preenchimento. A leitura “exatamente como” (comparação, c) não faz sentido, pois não há com o que comparar o preenchimento.

II (causa): As diary data were missing = “Como (já que) faltavam dados”: a falta de dados é a razão para calcular médias só para quem tinha cinco registros. Pode ser trocado por because, não por when (e).

III (comparação): the same exposure […] as interactive use = “a mesma exposição que o uso interativo”: a estrutura the same … as é de igualdade. Não é causa (b): o uso interativo não explica a exposição do uso passivo.

(a) inverte I e II.
questoes.dica: Dica: as tem vários sentidos. Comparação: the same … as, as … as, such as. Tempo: as = “quando/enquanto/à medida que”, muitas vezes com just as ou com verbos de ação pontual. Causa: as no início da frase seguido de um fato que justifica a oração principal (troque por “já que”). Teste cada substituição.

questoes.enunciado: Assinale a alternativa cujo segmento sublinhado expressa uma dedução dos autores, isto é, uma conclusão que eles apresentam como necessária a partir dos dados, e não uma possibilidade, uma obrigação ou uma recomendação.
alternativas: “part of the effect attributed to duration <u>might well</u> have been absorbed by it” (§17).
“It <u>must</u> also be borne in mind that the range of durations observed here was relatively narrow” (§17).
“students who were already sleeping poorly <u>may have</u> reached for their phones” (§18).
“Such efforts <u>should</u> give priority to students with an evening chronotype” (§24).
“students <u>must have</u> overestimated how long they slept” (§12).
questoes.explicacao:
Must have + particípio expressa dedução sobre o passado: como a duração declarada superou a do actígrafo em 23 minutos, os autores concluem que os estudantes “devem ter superestimado” (com certeza, certamente superestimaram) o próprio sono (§12). É (e).

(b) é a armadilha: o mesmo must, mas sem have + particípio e com voz passiva (must be borne in mind = “é preciso ter em mente”); indica necessidade/obrigação, não dedução. (a) might well have parece forte, mas é possibilidade, numa hipótese contrafactual (Had Marchetti-Oyelaran’s survey included…). (c) may have é possibilidade sobre o passado (a causalidade reversa cannot be ruled out). (d) should é recomendação.
questoes.dica: Dica: must have + particípio = dedução sobre o passado (“deve ter”, “com certeza”); may/might/could have + particípio = possibilidade sobre o passado. Must + verbo no infinitivo pode ser obrigação (must be borne in mind) ou dedução sobre o presente; decida pelo contexto. Outros sinais de dedução: is bound to, can only be explained by, it follows that.

questoes.enunciado:
Indique se os segmentos a seguir estão em acordo (A) ou desacordo (D) com o que apresentam os parágrafos 17 a 20.

  • (  )Na amostra, dormir pouco e dormir mal estiveram apenas moderadamente relacionados, e parte de quem dormia menos de sete horas relatava, mesmo assim, um sono de boa qualidade.
  • (  )Os autores atribuem a ausência de efeito da privação grave de sono ao fato de ela ser menos comum entre universitários do que se costuma supor.
  • (  )Os estudantes matutinos, segundo os autores, tendem a ficar sonolentos independentemente do que estejam fazendo no celular.
  • (  )Os filtros de modo noturno poderiam melhorar de forma significativa a qualidade do sono, desde que direcionados aos estudantes vespertinos.

Assinale a sequência correta.
alternativas: A – D – A – A
A – D – A – D
A – A – A – D
D – D – A – D
A – D – D – D
questoes.explicacao:
1 (A): the two were only moderately correlated (r = .29), and a sizeable group of students slept fewer than seven hours while nonetheless reporting good sleep quality (§17).

2 (D): os autores não afirmam que a privação grave não tem efeito; dizem que ele não poderia ter sido detectado porque a faixa de durações era estreita: the range of durations observed here was relatively narrow, so that the effects of severe sleep restriction […] could not have been detected (§17). A raridade aparece na frase, mas não é a explicação dada.

3 (A): morning types tend to become drowsy regardless of what they are doing on their phones (§19).

4 (D): a condição (provided that they are targeted at evening types) e a melhora (could produce meaningful improvements in sleep quality) referem-se às intervenções breves de interromper o uso interativo ou deixar o celular fora do quarto (§20). Os filtros de modo noturno são citados como conselho das campanhas que os autores consideram pouco eficaz.
questoes.dica: Dica: nos itens da discussão, desconfie quando o item junta peças verdadeiras de frases diferentes (a condição de uma proposta aplicada a outra) ou troca a explicação (“não houve efeito” × “não seria possível detectar”). Confira de que sujeito se fala e qual é a relação de causa que o texto realmente estabelece.

questoes.enunciado:
Considere os segmentos a seguir.

I - “smartphones, laptops and tablets have been steadily colonising the period between dinner and sleep” (§1) II - “the time students spent on their phones may have been underestimated” (§21) III - “Objective logging of device activity, which has become technically feasible with the consent of participants” (§22)

Os segmentos sublinhados estão, respectivamente, nos seguintes tempos e vozes verbais:
alternativas: presente perfeito contínuo, ativa – modal perfeito, passiva – presente perfeito, ativa.
presente perfeito, passiva – modal perfeito, passiva – presente perfeito, ativa.
presente perfeito contínuo, ativa – modal perfeito, ativa – presente perfeito, ativa.
presente perfeito contínuo, ativa – modal perfeito, passiva – passado perfeito, ativa.
presente perfeito, passiva – modal perfeito, ativa – presente perfeito, ativa.
questoes.explicacao:
I have been colonising: have been + verbo em -ing = presente perfeito contínuo, voz ativa (os aparelhos vêm ocupando o período). A armadilha (b, e) é ler have been como início de passiva; a passiva exigiria particípio (have been colonised).

II may have been underestimated: modal + have been + particípio = modal perfeito na voz passiva (o tempo “pode ter sido subestimado”). (c) e (e) erram a voz.

III has become: has + particípio de become, sem be = presente perfeito, ativa. Não é passado perfeito (d), que usaria had.
questoes.dica: Dica: depois de have/has been, olhe a forma seguinte. Com -ing é presente perfeito contínuo, voz ativa; com particípio é presente perfeito na passiva. Modal + have + particípio é modal perfeito ativo (could have influenced); modal + have been + particípio é modal perfeito passivo. Has marca presente perfeito; had, passado perfeito.

questoes.enunciado:
Considere as afirmações a seguir sobre a seção Limitations and Future Research (§21–§22).

I - Embora o desenho prospectivo garanta que a qualidade do sono foi medida antes das notas, o caráter observacional do estudo não exclui que fatores não medidos, como a conscienciosidade, tenham afetado sono e desempenho. II - A semana do diário, ainda que escolhida por ser típica, pode não ter captado as oscilações que ocorrem perto dos períodos de provas. III - Como a taxa de resposta inicial ficou abaixo de 50%, os autores supõem que os participantes eram menos interessados no tema do sono do que os não participantes. IV - O registro objetivo da atividade nos aparelhos eliminaria a dependência do autorrelato, mas os autores observam que ainda não é tecnicamente viável.

Estão de acordo com o texto as afirmações
alternativas: I, II e IV, apenas.
I, II e III, apenas.
II e III, apenas.
I e II, apenas.
I e IV, apenas.
questoes.explicacao:
I (correta): although the prospective design ensured that sleep quality was measured before grades were awarded, the study remains observational, and unmeasured variables such as conscientiousness or depressive symptoms could have influenced both sleep and achievement (§21).

II (correta): the diary covered a single week which, although it had been selected to be typical, may not have captured the variation that occurs around examination periods (§21).

III (incorreta): a limitação é citada, mas o sentido é o oposto: students who chose to participate may have been more interested in sleep, or more conscientious, than those who did not (§21).

IV (incorreta): a primeira parte está certa (would remove the reliance on self-report), mas o texto diz que esse registro has become technically feasible (§22), isto é, já é viável.
questoes.dica: Dica: julgue cada afirmação separadamente e só depois olhe as alternativas. As falsas costumam começar com uma parte verdadeira e trocar um detalhe no final (mais × menos interessados; já viável × ainda inviável). Leia a afirmação inteira antes de marcá-la como certa.

questoes.enunciado: Qual alternativa sintetiza a CONCLUSÃO (§23–§24) a que chegam os autores do texto?
alternativas: A qualidade do sono, mais que sua duração, prediz as notas; o uso interativo de telas pesa por encurtar o sono, e as ações devem mirar o que se faz nas telas, priorizando os vespertinos.
A qualidade do sono, mais que sua duração, prediz as notas; o uso interativo pesa por piorar essa qualidade, e melhorar o sono dos vespertinos deve bastar para elevar seu desempenho.
A qualidade do sono, mais que sua duração, prediz as notas; o uso interativo pesa por piorar essa qualidade, e as ações devem mirar o que se faz nas telas, priorizando os vespertinos.
A qualidade do sono, mais que sua duração, prediz as notas; o uso interativo pesa por piorar essa qualidade, e as ações devem reduzir o tempo total de tela, priorizando os vespertinos.
A qualidade do sono, mais que sua duração, prediz as notas; o uso interativo e o passivo pesam sobre essa qualidade, e as ações devem mirar o que se faz nas telas, priorizando os vespertinos.
questoes.explicacao:
(c) reúne as frases da conclusão: the quality of sleep, rather than the number of hours slept, is what predicts end-of-semester grades, and that evening screen use matters chiefly through its effect on sleep quality and only when it takes an interactive form (§23); focus on what students do on their screens, and when, than on how long they use them e give priority to students with an evening chronotype (§24).

Todas as alternativas começam igual; o erro está no meio ou no fim. (a) troca o caminho: o efeito passa pela qualidade, não pela duração (chiefly through its effect on sleep quality). (b) contradiz sleep should be regarded as one contributor to academic success among many, not as a remedy for poor performance in itself (§24). (d) recomenda o que os autores criticam: Campaigns that address screen time as a single undifferentiated quantity will therefore miss the distinction (§23). (e) inclui o uso passivo, que showed no association with either sleep or grades (§23).
questoes.dica: Dica: quando as alternativas compartilham o início, não marque pela primeira frase. Divida cada uma em partes (achado, mecanismo, recomendação) e confira cada parte com uma frase da conclusão. Os distratores trocam o mecanismo, ampliam o alcance (“deve bastar”) ou recomendam o oposto do que o texto propõe.
